final_proof:
Let \(f^{\to}(A)=f[A]=\{f(a):a\in A\}\). We prove both implications.

Suppose first that \((S_2,\tau _2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1=(S_1,\tau _1)\). Choose a homeomorphism \(f:S_1\to S_2\) (if a homeomorphism is initially given in the opposite direction, take its inverse). Then \(f\) is bijective. If \(U\in\tau _1\), then
\[
 f[U]=(f^{-1})^{-1}[U]\in\tau _2,
\]
because the inverse map \(f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\) is continuous. Thus the restriction \(f^{\to}|_{\tau _1}\) maps \(\tau _1\) into \(\tau _2\). Moreover, for every \(V\in\tau _2\), continuity of \(f\) gives \(f^{-1}[V]\in\tau _1\), and surjectivity of \(f\) gives
\[
 f[f^{-1}[V]]=V.
\]
Hence \(f^{\to}|_{\tau _1}:\tau _1\to\tau _2\) is surjective.

Conversely, suppose there is a bijection \(f:S_1\to S_2\) such that \(f^{\to}|_{\tau _1}:\tau _1\to\tau _2\) is surjective. Since this is a mapping to \(\tau _2\) and is onto, we have
\[
 \tau _2=\{f[U]:U\in\tau _1\}. \tag{1}
\]
We first verify that \(\tau _2\) is a topology. Because \(f[\varnothing]=\varnothing\) and \(f[S_1]=S_2\), equation (1) implies that \(\varnothing,S_2\in\tau _2\). If \(\{V_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq\tau _2\), choose \(U_i\in\tau _1\) such that \(V_i=f[U_i]\). Direct images commute with arbitrary unions, so
\[
 \bigcup_{i\in I}V_i=f\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right]\in\tau _2.
\]
Finally, if \(V_1,V_2\in\tau _2\), write \(V_j=f[U_j]\) with \(U_j\in\tau _1\). Since \(f\) is injective,
\[
 V_1\cap V_2=f[U_1]\cap f[U_2]=f[U_1\cap U_2]\in\tau _2.
\]
Thus \(\tau _2\) satisfies the topology axioms (and closure under all finite intersections follows by induction).

It remains to show that \(f\) is a homeomorphism. It is already bijective. Given \(V\in\tau _2\), equation (1) supplies \(U\in\tau _1\) with \(V=f[U]\); injectivity of \(f\) then yields
\[
 f^{-1}[V]=f^{-1}[f[U]]=U\in\tau _1.
\]
Therefore \(f\) is continuous. On the other hand, for every \(U\in\tau _1\), equation (1) says \(f[U]\in\tau _2\), and
\[
 (f^{-1})^{-1}[U]=f[U].
\]
Consequently \(f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\) is continuous as well. Hence \(f\) is a homeomorphism and \((S_2,\tau _2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1\), as required.
